forces: Concert band; transcription by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: The United States Air Force Band plays the first movement of La Mer, “De l’aube à midi sur la mer”, in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement. The movement opens on a low B and moves to the broad D♭ major chords of noon.

sections.label: Intro · Short phrases over held low B
sections.mNote: Short phrases enter above a held bass note.

sections.label: A · D♭ major, six quavers to the bar
sections.mNote: Six quavers to the bar, with quick figures underneath.

sections.label: B · Rising figures and overlapping phrases
sections.mNote: Short phrases overlap above the moving accompaniment.

sections.label: C · New melody in four parts
sections.mNote: Four lines play the new melody together.

sections.label: D · Short phrases with softer replies
sections.mNote: The melody divides into shorter phrases between instruments.

sections.label: Link · Held notes before the chorale
sections.mNote: Long held notes and quiet phrases lead into the slower close.

sections.label: E · Closing theme, broader phrases
sections.mNote: The closing theme enters over continuing movement in the accompaniment.

sections.label: Coda · Chorale, D♭ major
sections.mNote: Broad chords close the movement in D♭.

cues.title: Opening over a low B
cues.text: A low B is held beneath the opening. Short phrases enter above it, separated by long rests. Debussy marks the passage Très lent (very slow), and the first notes enter one at a time.
cues.evidence: Debussy, La Mer, Durand full score, opening, printed pp. 143–145. The harmony and pacing belong to the composition; instrumental assignments in Odom’s transcription are omitted. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition in Burgundy, 1903
cues.text: In the summer of 1903 Debussy stayed with his parents-in-law in Burgundy, far from the coast. He began La Mer there, drawing on memories of childhood summers at Cannes.
cues.evidence: Composition in Burgundy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy). Childhood visits to Cannes: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: Main section in D♭ major, 6/8
cues.text: The main section of the movement is in D♭ major and 6/8. Debussy marks it Modéré, sans lenteur (moderate, without slowness). The short rising phrases now have a running accompaniment beneath them.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed p. 147: change to five flats and 6/8, Modéré, sans lenteur, with continuous semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hokusai print on the score cover
cues.text: Debussy chose Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa for the cover of the published score of La Mer.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s choice of Hokusai for the score is documented by Jacob Greenberg, https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. The print and score cover are reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy).

cues.title: Twos against threes
cues.text: Groups of two notes and groups of three cross throughout the movement. One phrase divides the beat evenly while another runs across it, and the cross-rhythm continues in the quieter passages. Jacob Greenberg identified this interplay of twos and threes as a feature of the whole first movement.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg identifies the persistent interplay of twos and threes throughout the first movement: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Four-part melody, rehearsal 9
cues.text: A new melody enters in four parts, marked Très rythmé (strongly rhythmic). Its lines rise in turn and overlap, forming a phrase much longer than the short figures of the opening.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 9, printed p. 161: the four-part melody. The note describes the written music without assigning Odom’s parts to particular instruments.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris performances, 1905 and 1908
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducted the première in Paris on 15 October 1905, and it was coolly received. Debussy conducted the work himself in Paris on 19 and 26 January 1908, and the audience received it more warmly.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note gives the première and Debussy’s Paris performances on 19 and 26 January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: Closing chorale in D♭ major
cues.text: The closing chorale moves in broad notes over quicker figures underneath. The score returns to Très lent. D♭ major, first reached after the introduction, returns for the ending.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 14 to the end of movement I, printed pp. 171–173: Très lent, chorale and D♭-major close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From B to D♭ major
transitions.from: Intro · Short phrases over held low B
transitions.to: A · D♭ major, six quavers to the bar
transitions.how: The harmony of the opening, centred on B, moves to D♭ major. The metre changes from 6/4 to 6/8, and the new section is marked Modéré, sans lenteur. The sustained bass and widely spaced calls of the introduction are followed by short phrases over continuous semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 146–147, from the accelerating introduction into the main 6/8. This describes the composition’s harmony and rhythm, without assigning instruments in the transcription.

transitions.title: The tune becomes a chorale
transitions.how: At Très lent, the chorale is set in broad, sustained notes that stretch across the bar. Quicker figures continue below it, so the movement has two speeds at once. The closing progression centres on D♭ major and ends with short, emphatic chords.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 14 to the end of movement I, printed pp. 171–173. The description is restricted to the musical writing shared by the original and the transcription.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
